Ray: Good morning, nerds! It's Thursday, November nineteenth, twenty twenty six, and this is Nerd News Radio.

Ray: Today's lead: a neural network that works out the shape of each layer while a metal part is still being printed.

Lead story

Ray: Okay, so the problem. In laser powder bed fusion, which is metal printing where a laser melts thin layers of powder, you'd love to check the part's geometry as it's built. Catch a deviation early, qualify parts more efficiently.

Ray: The usual way is image segmentation. Take a picture of the layer, and have software outline where the material is. Here's the catch. Those models get trained under certain lighting and image conditions, and then the appearance shifts. Different material, different machine setup. The paper calls that photometric out-of-distribution generalization. Plain words: does it still work when the pictures look different from the training pictures?

Ada: Which is the thing that bites you in a real factory. So what did they do?

Ray: They built a hybrid. A U-Net, which is a standard image segmentation network, with a graph neural network placed in its bottleneck, the compressed middle of the network. The abstract says this is the first exploration of that design for this job.

Ray: They compared it to a plain U-Net and to active contours, a classic segmentation method. They used two case studies with different lattice geometries, materials, and manufacturing setups. And X-ray computed tomography gave the reference geometries.

Ada: So the ground truth is a scan, not a human drawing outlines. Good. And the result?

Ray: The hybrid got higher reconstruction accuracy and consistency than both benchmarks, and the gap grew when training and inference conditions differed. That held in both case studies and under controlled image perturbations.

Ada: Two case studies is not a lot. Does it work on any printer?

Ray: The abstract doesn't say. It also doesn't give the actual accuracy numbers in the part I have, or speak to speed or real-time use.

Ada: So is this catching defects?

Ray: Not claimed. It reconstructs geometry. Catching problems earlier is the hoped-for benefit, and that's an inference. Still, robustness to image shifts is exactly what you need before anyone trusts this on a shop floor.

Magnets and materials

Ray: On to magnets and materials. First, a study on which chemical elements matter most for training materials models.

Ray: Using a pretrained crystal-graph encoder, they ranked elements by how much useful supervision their compounds provide. Remove compounds with the top six ranked elements, and formation-energy errors rise by about one hundred to one hundred ten milli-electron-volts per atom. Bandgap errors rise by forty-two to eighty-five milli-electron-volts. Remove six lower-ranked elements, and little changes.

Ada: Does that hold for magnetic properties?

Ray: Not tested. The abstract covers formation energy and bandgap, so magnetism is unknown.

Ray: Second, a comparison of ways to choose which data to label, from random sampling to several active learning methods. Uncertainty-based sampling generally wins, but the best choice depends on the model, the dataset, and the task.

Ada: So, generally wins, not always wins. Fair.

Ray: Third, Matlantis released version nine of its machine-learning interatomic potential, called P F P. Training now covers ninety six elements, including the rare earths from praseodymium through lutetium. Formation energies for crystals with the new elements match experimental enthalpies about as well as for the older ones. And on the same A one hundred graphics card, forces are three to four times faster than a public competitor, with five to ten times as many atoms.

Ada: Anything on magnetic anisotropy?

Ray: Nothing. The abstract is silent on that.

Metal printing

Ray: Metal printing desk. First, neural operators as fast stand-ins for keyhole laser melting simulations. These are trained on FLOW three D simulations, and the best model has under two percent temperature error on straight tracks, about five percent with two to four beams. Inference takes under a second per time step.

Ada: But that's agreement with a simulation, not a printer.

Ray: Right. Though the solver settings were validated against published measurements, and predicted melt-pool depths at held-out conditions land within thirty percent of published values.

Ada: Thirty percent is generous.

Ray: It is. Next, single-crystal growth of nickel superalloys by laser directed energy deposition. Adjusting laser power from infrared thermal feedback, plus simulation-guided cooling, nearly doubled the continuous single-crystal build height compared with process control alone. Electron backscatter diffraction confirmed it.

Ray: And Dyndrite added direct scan-card control for Xact Metal's two hundred G machines, so users can program native arcs and other curved toolpaths.

Weird physics corner

Ray: Okay, my favorite. The central limit theorem says sums of random things look Gaussian. At a critical point, with long-range correlations, that breaks. So does any general law survive for rare fluctuations?

Ray: Researchers used Tethered Monte Carlo on the two-dimensional Ising model and reached probabilities as small as one in a one followed by two hundred zeros. Normalized by width, the far tails collapse onto a single curve shared by different models in the same universality class.

Ada: Two hundred zeros. I've never been that sure of anything, including my coffee order.

Ray: The amplitude is compatible with a conjecture derived from conformal field theory, and points toward a generalized central limit theorem. Compatible, note, not proven.

Ray: Also, a proposal called local semiclassical gravity. Gravity is sourced by the quantum state of a local region, updated only by measurements in its past light cone. It recovers the Schrödinger Newton equation at low speeds and avoids faster-than-light signalling.

Ada: A proposal, not an experiment.

Ray: Exactly.

Graph-augmented U-Net improves in-situ LPBF geometry reconstruction under image shifts

arXiv · AM monitoring & physics · 9/10

The abstract reports a U-Net combined with a graph neural network that reconstructs the shape of each layer during laser powder bed fusion metal printing. It says the method beats a plain U-Net and active contours when conditions differ between training and use, checked against X-ray CT reference geometries on two case studies. The general appeal is seeing a part's shape while it is printed, which could help catch problems earlier; that benefit is an inference, not a claim from the abstract.

Rare critical fluctuations in 2D Ising collapse onto a universal tail

arXiv · spin models & criticality · 7/10

Using a method called Tethered Monte Carlo, the abstract reports measuring order-parameter fluctuations with probabilities as small as 10^-200. The normalised tails collapse onto one curve across models in the 2D Ising class. The authors say the amplitude agrees with a conformal-field-theory conjecture and points to a generalised central limit theorem at criticality, a sharp test of theory about how rare events behave at a phase transition.

DoW and Commerce launch nationwide assessment of barriers to defense AM

News · AM policy & funding · 7/10

The Department of War announced a nationwide assessment of barriers to additive manufacturing (3D printing) in defense production, and ExecutiveGov covers a related survey from the Department of War and Commerce. Only headlines are available, so scope, deadlines and eligibility are unconfirmed. Assessments like this can shape which technologies get funding and qualification effort.

ChinaTalk asks whether a new Congress will change rare-earth policy

News · rare earths & magnets policy · 8/10

ChinaTalk asks whether the new Congress will shift rare-earth policy. Only the headline is available, so the specific proposals are unconfirmed. Rare earths are key ingredients in strong permanent magnets, which go into electric motors, defense hardware and many other products, so the question has wide consequences.

Constrained Luttinger–Tisza treatment of single-Q spiral magnets

arXiv · spin models & criticality · 7/10

The abstract reports a method that enforces fixed spin lengths within the Luttinger–Tisza approach, a standard way to find ground-state magnetic orders in models of exchange interactions. For bilinear spin models with one or two sublattices, it reports that enforcing local circularity can shift the preferred ordering wave vector. It is a theory tool for predicting magnetic structures from exchange couplings, aimed at spiral orders.

ML · Magnetic Materials

Euler-characteristic observable shows order-parameter-like behavior in 2D Ising

arXiv · magnetism + ML · 6/10

The abstract reports a topological measure, the Euler characteristic, that behaves like an order parameter in the 2D Ising model. Using multihistogram reweighting and finite-size scaling, its pseudocritical temperatures converge to the known critical temperature on square and triangular lattices. Its exponent estimate depends more on the fitting range than magnetization does, which the authors attribute to stronger subleading corrections. It is a statistical-physics study rather than a materials application.

Pretrained crystal-graph encoder ranks which elements give transferable supervision

arXiv · ML materials discovery · 6/10

The abstract reports that removing compounds containing the encoder's six top-ranked elements raises prediction errors by roughly 100–110 meV per atom and 42–85 meV on formation-energy and bandgap tasks. The finding suggests some elements carry much of the useful training signal for materials models. The abstract does not test magnetic targets, so whether it carries over to magnetism is unknown.

Uncertainty-based sampling generally wins in comparison of training-data acquisition strategies

arXiv · ML materials discovery · 6/10

The abstract reports a systematic comparison of strategies for choosing which data to label, from random sampling to several active-learning methods. It says uncertainty-based sampling generally does best, but that the winner depends on model, dataset and task. The authors offer guidance for a given labelling budget, which matters most when labelled data is expensive.

Matlantis PFP v9 extends r2SCAN training to Pr–Lu and 96 elements

arXiv · ML materials discovery · 5/10

Matlantis's PFP v9 machine-learning potential extends training to 96 elements, including the rare-earth range from praseodymium to lutetium. The abstract reports formation energies for crystals with newly supported elements that match experimental enthalpies as well as older elements do, and faster inference than SevenNet-Omni. It is a tool for simulating atomic structures, and the abstract says nothing about magnetic anisotropy.

Additive Manufacturing

Neural-operator surrogates for keyhole laser melting with provenance tracking

arXiv · ML for manufacturing · 6/10

The abstract reports FNO, RIGNO and GAOT neural-operator surrogates trained on FLOW-3D simulations of keyhole laser melting, with errors below about 2–5% on held-out simulations. Melt-pool and vapor-depression depths at held-out conditions fall within 30% of published values. Because these are fast stand-ins for physics simulations rather than direct measurements, their value lies in quick prediction.

IR-feedback power control extends single-crystal L-DED growth to nearly double height

arXiv · AM monitoring & physics · 6/10

The abstract reports that adjusting laser power in real time from infrared thermal feedback, combined with simulation-guided cooling, nearly doubled the continuous epitaxial build height. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) validated the single-crystal result. It is a closed-loop control example with metallurgical ground truth, focused on nickel superalloys.

Dyndrite adds direct scan-card control for Xact Metal LPBF machines

3D Printing Industry · 5/10

Dyndrite LPBF Pro now supports native arcs and non-linear toolpaths on the XM200G and XM200G µHD metal printers. It is a machine-capability update that lets software drive curved scan paths directly. It is most relevant to researchers who control scan paths in their experiments.

Theoretical Physics

Potts order preempts a 2-form U(1) spin liquid in 3D spin vorticity models

arXiv · spin models & criticality · 7/10

The abstract reports that height locking maps to a 3-state Potts antiferromagnet, giving weak all-in–all-out order in the pyrochlore model, and that all three models show a 3D Ising transition. The spin liquid survives only at intermediate length scales. It links frustrated magnets to Ising-type transitions, a recurring theme in statistical physics.

Local semiclassical gravity: a causal version of Schrödinger–Newton

arXiv · quantum physics · 6/10

In plain terms, the proposal lets gravity be sourced by the quantum state of a local region, updated only by measurements in that region's past light cone, instead of quantizing gravity itself. The abstract says this recovers the Schrödinger–Newton equation at low speeds and avoids faster-than-light signalling. Physicists care because it tests whether gravity must be quantum at all. It is a proposal, not an experimental result.

APS: Hawking's information paradox exposed a clash between theories

APS Physics · 7/10

This APS Physics piece marks 50 years since Hawking's information paradox was raised. The puzzle is that black-hole evaporation seems to destroy quantum information, which clashes with quantum mechanics. Resolving it likely requires a theory that joins gravity and quantum mechanics. Only a short summary is available, so details are unconfirmed.

Domain walls in a frustrated spin chain behave as tunable quantum particles

arXiv · spin models & criticality · 6/10

The abstract reports DMRG calculations for a frustrated spin-1/2 XXZ chain with bond alternation, where a chirality domain wall acts like a particle in a box. Its mass grows by over two orders of magnitude and diverges near δ*≈0.012. It is a one-dimensional theory study, but a clean example of how competing exchange interactions can tune quantum excitations.

Production Engineering Solutions reports a world-first Nadcap approval for GKN Aerospace's wire-fed laser directed energy deposition process (L-DED-w).
